Biddy the infamous ‘truck-eating’ bridge

By: Annalise Lubbe | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The town of Muizenberg is synonymous with surfing. But a new kind of fame has surfaced: a bridge with an appetite for trucks, taking a bite out of their roofs as they try to squeeze underneath.

Unique Selling Point:
Bridget, or Biddy for short, has become a regular name in traffic bulletins. Time and time again, trucks misjudge her height and get wedged underneath, causing major traffic jams and of course serious damage to the ill-fated trucks.

Biddy the bridge was built way back in 1910, as part of the rail network to connect cities in South Africa. In those days, ox wagons were the primary mode of transport, and so the bridge was built with a clearance of only 2.5 meters. Fast forward to the present day, and delivery trucks are buzzing through the streets all the time. But unfortunately, Biddy has not moved with the times, and almost weekly she claims one or two unsuspected trucks, whose drivers did not adhere to the warning signs placed on both sides of the bridge.


Summary:
Muizenberg is a colourful village with people from all walks of life, most famous for its Surfers’ Corner. The bridge affectionately known as Biddy can be found in the heart of the town. She has become a notorious part of the personality of Muizenberg.

People who have made a home for themselves underneath the bridge say that they sometimes even try to warn oncoming trucks to turn around, as they know an accident is about to happen. One such character is Ibrahiem Cassiem who has witnessed this many times. Ibraham says it sounds like a 'boom' and then you know, chaos is around the corner.

At a surf shop close by, Tessa Moore and her husband Peter, who have been running the shop since the 70s, have become quite fond of Biddy. They created a Facebook page for the bridge, which has attracted 4000 followers who are keen to get updates about Biddy’s latest victims.

Truida Prekel, now in her eighties, lives on the 6th floor of a neighbouring building, and has been taking photos of Biddy-related incidents for many years. She has a wealth of stories to tell about the comedic scenes she has witnessed over the years.

Then there is Chris Taylor, a guide and historian who conducts tours for visitors to the town. Part of his tour naturally looks at Biddy’s history. As luck would have it, sometimes Chris will be standing right next to the bridge and telling her story, when she proves him right and a truck gets stuck as his tour group looks on in disbelief.

The Cape Town municipality has implemented several systems and warning signs over the years to reduce the number of incidents, to no avail. It seems the only options are to raise the bridge, or to lower the road. Both solutions are extremely costly and impractical and will involve major changes to the underlying infrastructure.


Further information:
Over the years, the railway bridge crossing Atlantic Road in Muizenberg has claimed many victims: truck drivers who don’t know their own height and wedge their vehicles underneath the bridge. This causes enormous traffic congestion and hours of delays.

Despite reports in 2018 that the City of Cape Town installed an Intelligent Transport System (ITS) to reduce the number of incidents, many truck drivers do not take the warnings seriously, or perhaps they simply do not see them.

The ITS system detects the actual height of a vehicle. Any truck that won’t make the 2.5 meter clearance will cause the board at the intersection to flash for about 30 seconds notifying the driver to turn right rather than left.

In the 70s and 80s there were actual chains barricading the road, but these were apparently removed for fear that someone would not see them and write off their vehicle, with the potential for expensive lawsuits.

The simple truth is that this old road is just not made for trucks. She wasn’t even made for motor vehicles. She was made for ox wagons.

Biddy’s best – or worst – week was in December 2017. On Monday, she snacked on a Checkers delivery truck. She enjoyed the flavour so much that she had a second helping on Wednesday. And then, just to keep things interesting, she tried a Shoprite truck for dessert on Thursday.

Signs and sensors have been installed near the bridge to warn drivers but not much else can be done. The bridge is owned by the railroad, and they won’t pay to raise it. As for lowering the road, a sewer line runs beneath it, so that’s not an option either.

So nothing can come up and nothing can come down, and the municipality just keeps on trying the same thing over and over again and expecting a different result.

The story
We spend a day in Muizenberg to hear the stories from everyone and hear what the City of Cape Town has to say.

The story is told in a quirky way. The colourful characters of Muizenberg share their own stories with us and their take on Biddy the bridge. There have been many traffic warnings about accidents at the bridge and two radio talk shows discussing possible solutions. But they also point out that some residents do not want to see Biddy change.

We will use the audio track of the traffic reports and short sound ups of the interviews to give it energy and life. There are also dozens of photos which we will have access to, as well as the Facebook page with all the comments from followers.

We cannot plan for an accident to happen and so will have to rely on the archive visuals to show the accidents. Truida Prekel will tell us some of the stories of the pictures she took to give it presence and Ibrahiem, who is living underneath the bridge, will tell us how he experienced it. Then the historian will put it in perspective and finally, Tessa and her husband, who own the surf shop, share their thoughts about Biddy and what they have witnessed over the years and Chris Taylor will give a brief glimps of the history behind Biddy.

A link will show us the vibrant bungalows and the beach to establish the surfing scene synonymous with Muizenberg, and a link at the ITS board will show how trucks should move into the right-hand lane when the warning sign comes up, and finally a link at the bridge to show the hammering old Biddy has endured over the years. There is still a piece of metal from a truck stuck in the wall above the bridge.

Bernard Oosthuizen, head of Transport Network Technology, will be the representative of the City of Cape Town. He will talk about the systems they have put in place and possible future plans which might help to reduce incidents.

Script:


FINAL SCRIPT - Biddy the bridge

Muizenberg early morning sequence

Up sound “EWN traffic - Happening in traffic this morning. We have a truck stuck under the railway bridge”...

V/O Traffic, the bane of our existence, even in beautiful Cape Town. Not even the sleepy surfing town of Muizenberg is immune.

Audio up: “Please adhere to all the traffic signage in this area. I am Zain Johnson for Eyewitness news traffic.”

V/O We’re here to meet someone at the center of a long-standing controversy. Someone small in stature but with a big appetite. Someone or - more precisely - something making waves here in the southern suburbs.

Link: In the center of the town, just around the corner from the beach, there is a bridge…She has made quite a name for herself, and that name is Bridget or Biddy for short.

Up music

V/O It is a quaint name for someone with such an insatiable appetite…for trucks that is.

Truida Prekel: I don’t think there has ever been a month that there has not been an incident. So we see it as Bridget having breakfast or lunch or supper. But there are days where she has two meals.

V/O Truida Prekel lives on the 6th floor of Muizenberg’s tallest building. You might say that’s given her a prime seat at Biddy’s table - and she has documented quite a few of those meals.

Derek Watts: Tell us about some of the stories.

Truida Prekel: One that is really funny is a guy that had a tall fishing rod and he got stuck underneath. And then in the water crisis everyone was buying water tanks and so one guy came with a delivery of 4 or 5 water tanks and he thought he was going to get through.

V/O No surprise how that turned out.

Up music

V/O But Biddy hasn’t always been this controversial. After all, she's one of Muizenberg’s oldest residents.

Link: Bridget was born during the era of the horse and carriage and steam trains. But which came first Bridget or the railway line?

Chris Taylor: Bridget began life, probably 1910. The railway came through Muizenberg to Simon’s Town in 1882 it was opened. There was so much traffic traveling to Muizenberg that they doubled the line in 1910. And that’s when the bridge was built.

V/O Chris Taylor is a respected local historian, and an unashamed Biddy fan.

Up train sound

Derek Watts: So the original line came before Bridget?

Chris Taylor: It did…. There were no motorcars at the time but when the rail arrived they said ‘make it sturdy’ we will make it fit for life. And she is still standing.

Up music …

V/O Just around the corner from Biddy, Tessa Moore and her partner, Peter run their renowned surf shop.

Tessa Moore; Bridget has been eating trucks since, well certainly, Peter opened his shop in July 71 and he said within two weeks he heard this ‘kaboom’, and thought the world had come to an end and everybody said ‘not that is just the bridge.’ so it has been a constant source of amusement ever since then.

V/O But what’s celebrity status without proper publicity? Tessa set up a Facebook page and, while we’re not talking Beyonce numbers, this shy, little bridge now has 4000 online friends.

Pause

V/O On average Biddy munches her way through two trucks per month. But in late 2017, she set a personal record.

Tessa Moore: Tessa; Oh that was amazing that would have Whitey Basson, owner of Shoprite in tears. Within 3 or 4 days she had a checkers food services. She had a checkers truck and she had a shoprite truck.

Derek Watts: Checkmate for Bridget?

Tessa Moore: Absolutely.

V/O It was time to talk specifics with someone from the City.

Bernard Oosthuizen: Head: Transport Network Technology - City of Cape Town:
The normal bridge, our provincial standard, is 5.2 meters and this bridge is less than half than that. We detect it at 2.4 to have a safety margin.

Derek Watts: So it is a lot lower?

Bernard Oosthuizen: It is less than half. And she is one of many in the world.

V/O And her international competitors have equally impressive appetites like this one in the US - a little taller than Biddy - nicknamed “the can-opener,” for obvious reasons.

Up music over a sequence of truck incidents.

V/O So with Biddy pouncing on any truck foolish enough to try and squeeze its way under her, why not simply lower the road or raise the bridge?

Bernard Oosthuizen: That’s the question everyone asks. This bridge was built approximately ten years before the first car. So to lift a railway line by 2.5meters to the national standard is going to be impossible.

V/O Lowering the road isn’t an option either because of cabling and other services.
City of Cape town officials have spent years searching for solutions. What they’ve come up with is a 3D laser system that detects the dimensions of approaching vehicles and warns anyone too high to take an alternative route. But is it working?

Bernard Oosthuizen: In the last ten years there are 36% more trucks on the road. So there will always be people who don’t adhere to road signs unfortunately.

V/O And when those signs are ignored, Truida is one of the first to hear the result. I say one because there are people even closer to the action.

Truida Prekel: It's interesting. When I hear the bash then immediately I hear laughter.

V/O The source of the laughter is the homeless for whom Biddy provides shelter.

Truida Prekel: On a few occasions, they have seen a lorry come, knowing this is trouble coming and they have stopped them.

Ibrahiem Cassiem: There is even signs there when you come in but they overlooked it. (There are even signs at the entrance, but they ignore them). They just come in. (They just keep going.) Sometimes I am trying to stop them, (Sometimes, I try to stop them saying, it’s too high,) saying “hello” it’s too high yah. They just think “ag man.” (but they just think “ag man.”)

V/O Ibrahiem Cassiem has been living here for almost 15 years.

Derek Watts: Now Bridget is your home.

Ibrahiem Cassiem: Yeah, it's my home. That is the love of my life.

Ibrahiem Cassiem: Sometimes when the water is running from the wall (Sometimes when the water runs down the wall) then I think “ah Bridget is crying” (Then I think Bridget is crying,) because she experienced a lot of things. (because she has experienced many things:) Happiness, laughter, crying tears, sadness. (happiness, laughter, crying tears, sadness…) If only she could talk yah! (If only she could speak.)

Chris Taylor: In a humble way, she is notorious. Others came to be truck eaters as well but nothing quite like Bridget. She is consistent.

V/O Consistent, loved, loathed. For now a fixture in Muizenberg but for how much longer?
_____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
PROMOS
Promo 1: 22 Seconds
V/O There is a resident in Muizenberg - diminutive in stature - who is causing quite a stir: an old stately bridge built at a time of horse and cart who does not tolerate huge trucks trying to squeeze through.
Chris Taylor: In a humble way, she is notorious. Others came to be truck eaters as well but nothing quite like Bridget. She is consistent, you know.

Promo 2: 22 Seconds
V/O She has an insatiable appetite for large trucks and has earned herself the nickname of the truck-eater. She is a shy little bridge in the center of Muizenberg called Bridget or Biddy for short.
Truida Prekel: I would say I don’t think there has ever been a month that there has not been an incident. So we see it as Bridget having breakfast or lunch or supper.

Promo 3: 11 Seconds
V/O Muizenberg is synonymous with surfing. But a shy little bridge built more than a hundred years ago, has claimed a celebrity status with her regular truck munching antics.
_____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Sunday promo
Derek: She is a regular name in traffic bulletins.

EWN traffic: “Happening in traffic this morning. We have a truck stuck under the railway bridge crossing the Atlantic road in Muizenberg

Derek: Truck-eater, can-opener, top shaver, she has many names, but her real name is Bridget or Biddy for short. And you will find her in the heart of Muizenberg.

Tessa Moore: Within 3 or 4 days she had a checkers food services. She had a checkers truck and she had a shoprite truck.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The town of Muizenberg is synonymous with surfing. But a new kind of fame has surfaced: a bridge with an appetite for trucks, taking a bite out of their roofs as they try to squeeze underneath.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Bridget, or Biddy for short, has become a regular name in traffic bulletins. Time and time again, trucks misjudge her height and get wedged underneath, causing major traffic jams and of course serious damage to the ill-fated trucks. Biddy the bridge was built way back in 1910, as part of the rail network to connect cities in South Africa. In those days, ox wagons were the primary mode of transport, and so the bridge was built with a clearance of only 2.5 meters. Fast forward to the present day, and delivery trucks are buzzing through the streets all the time. But unfortunately, Biddy has not moved with the times, and almost weekly she claims one or two unsuspected trucks, whose drivers did not adhere to the warning signs placed on both sides of the bridge.
metadata.Summary: Muizenberg is a colourful village with people from all walks of life, most famous for its Surfers’ Corner. The bridge affectionately known as Biddy can be found in the heart of the town. She has become a notorious part of the personality of Muizenberg. People who have made a home for themselves underneath the bridge say that they sometimes even try to warn oncoming trucks to turn around, as they know an accident is about to happen. One such character is Ibrahiem Cassiem who has witnessed this many times. Ibraham says it sounds like a 'boom' and then you know, chaos is around the corner. At a surf shop close by, Tessa Moore and her husband Peter, who have been running the shop since the 70s, have become quite fond of Biddy. They created a Facebook page for the bridge, which has attracted 4000 followers who are keen to get updates about Biddy’s latest victims. Truida Prekel, now in her eighties, lives on the 6th floor of a neighbouring building, and has been taking photos of Biddy-related incidents for many years. She has a wealth of stories to tell about the comedic scenes she has witnessed over the years. Then there is Chris Taylor, a guide and historian who conducts tours for visitors to the town. Part of his tour naturally looks at Biddy’s history. As luck would have it, sometimes Chris will be standing right next to the bridge and telling her story, when she proves him right and a truck gets stuck as his tour group looks on in disbelief. The Cape Town municipality has implemented several systems and warning signs over the years to reduce the number of incidents, to no avail. It seems the only options are to raise the bridge, or to lower the road. Both solutions are extremely costly and impractical and will involve major changes to the underlying infrastructure.
metadata.Further information: Over the years, the railway bridge crossing Atlantic Road in Muizenberg has claimed many victims: truck drivers who don’t know their own height and wedge their vehicles underneath the bridge. This causes enormous traffic congestion and hours of delays. Despite reports in 2018 that the City of Cape Town installed an Intelligent Transport System (ITS) to reduce the number of incidents, many truck drivers do not take the warnings seriously, or perhaps they simply do not see them. The ITS system detects the actual height of a vehicle. Any truck that won’t make the 2.5 meter clearance will cause the board at the intersection to flash for about 30 seconds notifying the driver to turn right rather than left. In the 70s and 80s there were actual chains barricading the road, but these were apparently removed for fear that someone would not see them and write off their vehicle, with the potential for expensive lawsuits. The simple truth is that this old road is just not made for trucks. She wasn’t even made for motor vehicles. She was made for ox wagons. Biddy’s best – or worst – week was in December 2017. On Monday, she snacked on a Checkers delivery truck. She enjoyed the flavour so much that she had a second helping on Wednesday. And then, just to keep things interesting, she tried a Shoprite truck for dessert on Thursday. Signs and sensors have been installed near the bridge to warn drivers but not much else can be done. The bridge is owned by the railroad, and they won’t pay to raise it. As for lowering the road, a sewer line runs beneath it, so that’s not an option either. So nothing can come up and nothing can come down, and the municipality just keeps on trying the same thing over and over again and expecting a different result. The story We spend a day in Muizenberg to hear the stories from everyone and hear what the City of Cape Town has to say. The story is told in a quirky way. The colourful characters of Muizenberg share their own stories with us and their take on Biddy the bridge. There have been many traffic warnings about accidents at the bridge and two radio talk shows discussing possible solutions. But they also point out that some residents do not want to see Biddy change. We will use the audio track of the traffic reports and short sound ups of the interviews to give it energy and life. There are also dozens of photos which we will have access to, as well as the Facebook page with all the comments from followers. We cannot plan for an accident to happen and so will have to rely on the archive visuals to show the accidents. Truida Prekel will tell us some of the stories of the pictures she took to give it presence and Ibrahiem, who is living underneath the bridge, will tell us how he experienced it. Then the historian will put it in perspective and finally, Tessa and her husband, who own the surf shop, share their thoughts about Biddy and what they have witnessed over the years and Chris Taylor will give a brief glimps of the history behind Biddy. A link will show us the vibrant bungalows and the beach to establish the surfing scene synonymous with Muizenberg, and a link at the ITS board will show how trucks should move into the right-hand lane when the warning sign comes up, and finally a link at the bridge to show the hammering old Biddy has endured over the years. There is still a piece of metal from a truck stuck in the wall above the bridge. Bernard Oosthuizen, head of Transport Network Technology, will be the representative of the City of Cape Town. He will talk about the systems they have put in place and possible future plans which might help to reduce incidents. ______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
